doc.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013

title: Time Inc., the New York Times, the draft and Brandeis jazz concerts
summary: He wanted to be a journalist, worked at Time Inc. and the Times, was drafted, then at Brandeis edited the paper and arranged jazz via George Wein's Storyville.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: not much more than a glorified messenger but I got to meet a lot of people and actually was talked into running for office at the American Newspaper Guild, a pretty left wing thing. I was a Wallace — Henry Wallace was running for president. That was that famous election when Truman — Truman and Dewey. And it was a great experience because I was working at Time Inc. I was at a nerve center there on election night, which was a studio where they were broadcasting, and there was a guy named H.V. Kaltenborn, who was — he was something similar to the people they now have on Fox News now. You know, he was a real right winger and of course a great Dewey supporter. And as the news came in it was just amazing what was happening there, because nobody could believe it when it came in that Truman was winning. And Kaltenborn, who had a kind of complexion, he turned red as a beet. I thought he was going to have a heart attack or something. There was quite a way to — it was a great education for American politics. But anyway, then my father had become very friendly with the great cartoonist Al Hirschfeld, who had a circle of, you know, friends, a lot of the New York Times people. So my father, who had been, also been a theater critic and became friendly with Brooks Atkinson, who was the New York Times first string drama critic, and he used to take my father to openings because he said my father was the only person he knew who would not ask him at intermission, “Well what do you think,” you know, which is a terrible thing when somebody does not want that. So they became great friends. At first it got me a job as copy boy at the New York Times, which I didn’t realize then was a pretty big deal, you know, that’s very coveted. But at the time I’d been there about three months I got drafted. So when I got drafted my father was very nervous. Of course he had not been happy about my hanging out late at night, you know, sometimes even not coming home at all. Anyway he thought that I would not be fit for Army duty. But it was all right, so that was a kind of a sea change. And then when I came out I went on the GI bill, I went to Brandeis University. And even then I had no thoughts about getting into jazz in any kind of professional way, but I started — eventually I became editor of the school paper called The Justice, and there was a little — Brandeis was very new then. It started, and the first class was the class of, let’s see, ’52. And there were only about — all undergrads, no graduate school then, about 700 students, a wonderful faculty, and there was some money for student activities but a very few jazz fans got together and decided to get some money to bring jazz to campus. So we hooked up with George Wein who then was running Storyville. This was before Newport, just before, just at the cusp of Newport, actually the year Newport started — ’54. So we went to George and asked if we could ask some people who were appearing at Storyville to come to Brandeis. He said, “You can do it, get anybody you want.
